sections.heading: Hearing your call as a real invitation
sections.text: Lord God, you are the one who calls first. In your Word you say, “Come to me. Return to me.” Please do more than let me hear those words from the outside. Bring light into my heart so I know that your call is meant for sinners like me. Help me taste the kindness in your command, not only its authority: you invite the unworthy to come, you call me into fellowship with yourself, and every promise you make in the gospel rests on grace, not on what I can earn.
theological_themes: God initiates salvation by calling sinners through his Word.
The gospel command is both true and gracious, inviting the unworthy into fellowship with God.
God's promises are grounded in grace rather than human merit.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus personally invites the weary to come to him and receive rest, showing that the command to come is not cold or bare but full of mercy and welcome.
This passage calls the wicked to return to the Lord and grounds that return in God's abundant pardon, matching the prayer's emphasis on God's gracious invitation to sinners.
Paul describes God shining light into human hearts so people see the glory of God in Christ. That supports the prayer's request for inward illumination, not merely outward hearing.

sections.heading: Resting in the promise instead of digging for hidden answers
sections.text: So, Lord, keep me from getting lost in trying to figure out what you have not asked me to know first—whether I am chosen, whether I am loved, whether there is room for me. You have told me to turn to you, and you have promised that if I come, you will receive me. Christ offers himself to me; let me take him at his word. Pour out your Spirit on me, put sin to death in me, free me from condemnation, and give me strength to keep going until the end.
theological_themes: Assurance is sought through God's revealed gospel promise rather than speculation about election.
Christ receives those who come to him in faith.
The Spirit applies salvation by freeing from condemnation, killing sin, and sustaining perseverance.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus promises not to cast out anyone who comes to him. This directly grounds the prayer's confidence in Christ's open promise rather than anxious self-searching.
Paul joins freedom from condemnation with the Spirit's work of putting sin to death. This supports the prayer's link between pardon, the Spirit's power, and ongoing perseverance.
Paul's confidence that God will complete the work he began supports the prayer's request for strength to persevere as God's continuing work, not self-reliance.

sections.heading: Coming for grace when my heart is at its worst
sections.text: You are glad to help people who ask you for grace and come to you because they have nowhere else to go. When my heart is sour with sin, weighed down by sorrow, dark, and afraid of judgment, only your free grace can help me come low before you honestly. Teach me to stop defending myself. Let me feel the truth about my unworthiness without running away from you, because your mercy is my only hope.
theological_themes: Grace is given to the needy who come to God for mercy.
Conviction of sin should lead to humble return, not despair or self-defense.
Human unworthiness highlights the freeness of God's mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Because believers have a merciful high priest, they are invited to draw near for mercy and grace in need. This fits the prayer's movement toward God precisely when the heart feels most unworthy.
The tax collector comes to God with no defense except mercy, and Jesus says he goes home justified. That illustrates the deep abasement and grace-dependent approach requested here.

sections.heading: Repenting of neglect and religious self-deception
sections.text: Let me grieve that I so often forget to come to you day by day. Cleanse me from the dishonest habit of bringing my heart to religious duties because the activity itself pleases me, or because it seems reasonable and respectable, while I am not truly coming to you. Save me from using obedience as a way to avoid honest fellowship with you. Draw me back to yourself, not just to the motions of devotion.
theological_themes: Daily communion with God can be neglected even by religious activity.
God desires sincerity of heart, not merely outward duty.
Repentance includes confessing self-deception in spiritual practices.

scripture_references.connection: God rebukes worship that is outwardly near but inwardly distant. This supports the prayer's concern about performing duties without truly coming to God.
David acknowledges that God desires truth in the inward being, which grounds the request to be cleansed from hidden religious self-deception.
The promise of forgiveness and cleansing for confessed sin supports the prayer's appeal for God to cleanse not only obvious sins but deceitful motives.

sections.heading: Receiving your discipline without forgetting Christ
sections.text: If suffering is what you use to preserve me and make me holy, then let it be measured by your wisdom and love. Let every hard demand be suited to what my soul needs. Let every rod that falls be fitted by your hand—not to destroy me, but to correct me, humble me, and break what is proud and false in me. And when I feel the pain, do not let me look only at the rod. Help me see the Fatherly hand that holds it. Even more, do not let me forget the heavier blow that fell on Christ for me, the suffering that drew me to him and made my return possible.
theological_themes: God may use suffering as fatherly discipline for holiness.
Affliction should be interpreted under God's wise and loving hand, not as random destruction.
Christ's substitutionary suffering is the foundation of the believer's forgiveness and return to God.

scripture_references.connection: This passage teaches that God's discipline of his children is painful but purposeful, intended for holiness and peace. It directly supports the prayer's request to receive affliction as fitted by a Father's hand.

Peter connects Christ bearing sins with believers dying to sin and living to righteousness. This grounds the prayer's remembrance that Christ's suffering is what makes forgiveness and transformation possible.

Isaiah presents the Servant as wounded for the sins of others, with peace and healing coming through his suffering. This supports the prayer's image of the decisive blow falling on Christ for the believer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a Reformed framework in which election is real but assurance should be sought through the revealed gospel call and promise rather than by trying to inspect God's hidden decree. That framework is preserved without turning the prayer into an abstract discussion of predestination.

The original's request to be 'salted with suffering' and to receive a 'rod' fitted to the back reflects a Puritan view of affliction as fatherly chastisement. This can be pastorally sensitive, especially for severe trauma or abuse, so the adaptation frames suffering as something God may use wisely and lovingly, not as cruelty or as a simplistic explanation for every pain.

The phrase about the Spirit 'abolishing sin and punishment' could sound as if Christians become sinless immediately. The adaptation renders it as freedom from condemnation and the Spirit's ongoing work of putting sin to death, which better reflects the broader biblical already/not-yet pattern.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated the 'first act of calling' as God's outward call through Scripture and the 'second' as inward illumination by God, because the prayer distinguishes hearing the command from personally perceiving its sweetness and application.

I rendered 'I need not search to see if I am elect, or loved' as a refusal to begin with hidden questions rather than a denial of election. The point is pastoral assurance through coming to Christ, not curiosity about God's secret will.

I kept the concrete image of the rod but identified the hand holding it as Fatherly, because the original wants the sufferer to see God's personal providence behind discipline while also remembering the suffering borne by Christ.
